narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: A watchman awaits the beacon announcing Troy’s fall. Agamemnon’s victorious return will not restore a peaceful house: Clytemnestra kills him, and the sacrifice of Iphigenia stands among the grievances that the play brings home from war.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the source does
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translation; whitespace normalized): “Palace stand statues of the gods, and altars prepared for sacrifices._ _A Watchman_ I pray the gods to quit me of my toils, To close the watch I keep, this livelong year; For as a watch-dog lying, not at rest, Propped on one arm, upon the palace-roof Of Atreus’ race, too long, too well I know The starry”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Interpretation: Agamemnon’s return is the anti-Odyssey: the damaged house is not restored but fully exposed.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: The opening Watchman’s relief is not the play’s final judgement on victory. Read forward into the damaged household before assuming that a successful war guarantees a safe return.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: Heroic success abroad does not settle moral damage at home.

quiz.prompt: What signal does the Watchman await?
quiz.explanation: A beacon announcing Troy’s fall. Revisit the named passage and distinguish its narrative from the lesson’s interpretation.

quiz.prompt: Why is victory an insecure ending here?

choices.text: The Greek army has not yet sailed for Troy.
Clytemnestra is absent from the play.
The returning king faces violence and unresolved grievances at home.
